title: Years on the Steamer Madison pleasure boat on Lake Pontchartrain
summary: Contract with the Madison from West End to Mandeville and Madisonville; owners, passengers, schedule, weather and where the band played.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Working the Streckfus riverboats with Fate Marable

blocks.x: Me, you, the four pieces I think it was. Men, my chef on piano, and I played trumpet bass. I played with so many. You know what I mean? It's hard to keep it straight. It's hard to keep it straight. You know I played with so many of them. And sometimes you know you'll have one playing tonight and then you know anything, you've got to get another one to play with. That's the way it was going you know. It still is that way, actually isn't it? Still that way. You look for the man, that man going to come and he ain't showed up and then you've got to get somebody else. That's the way it went. All the bands that I played around with. That's the way it was. I even had trouble like that playing on the steam of Madison Boat. I told them, I said, now if you can't play regular let me know because I had to have a contract, which I did. It's a contract for the whole year. And my boat started running every Easter. That's when we started.
Where did that boat dock, Sadie?
West End. West End. West End.
Do you remember the company that owned that boat?

Well Mr. Devonport was his first name. He and his brother-in-law. He and his brother-in-law was two white guys, Mr. Devonport and his brother-in-law was named, I don't know, I think they were rich people.
Did they own other boats besides the Madison?
No, that's the only one, that's Pleasure Boat. The only boat they owned was that one. They would carry five hundred passengers and then they'd carry five hundred cars down on the deck.
Where would you play?

We'd run from the West End and we'd stop at Mandeville, then we'd stop at Madisonville, we'd put up at Madisonville. Sometime the ball, pardon me, ball game, you know they'd have a ball game over there, we'd bring a load over there on that. Sometime we'd have the newspaper men, we'd bring a load over there. Some of them get off at Mandeville, then we'd have to come back and pick them up.
What time would they leave in the morning?
We'd leave in the morning. We'd leave around about, somewhere around about nine o'clock in the morning. Then we'd be going for the whole day.
Yeah, what time would you get over to, where'd you stop in Madisonville first? No, we stopped in Mandeville first.
And then from Mandeville we'd go into Madisonville. Cause sometimes the people that have chartered the boat, some of them going to Mandeville, some going to Madisonville.
Okay, how long would it take you to get from West End over to Mandeville?
It didn't take long, maybe about a half hour. Oh that's long?
About a half hour. What would happen if you ran into, did you ever run into any storms when you were going across? Well it'd get rough sometimes.
The old boy would go to rock and roll, he'd go to play in the rock and two with it.
Were there times when they wouldn't go out because the weather was too bad?

Well no. We was lucky we never did have that kind of weather, you know what I mean? Going out with the boat. It would get rough out there in the river. We'd get rough with them playing. Everybody would say, ooh, you hear that water coming, them waves coming over the deck. That's true.
You were playing out on the deck?

No, we played up on the second deck. Inside. Yeah, inside, yeah. And downstairs is where they, at the deck where they had the cars parked. And up on the second deck is where the people sit, the games, you know. They had a bar up there?
Everything.
